html:
The meeting house of a confraternity of wealthy Venetian citizens, founded in 1478 and named after Saint Roch, a protector against plague, whose relics lie in the church next door. It stands in the San Polo district of Venice, a few steps from the Frari. The building was begun in 1515 by Pietro Bon and passed through three more architects before it was finished in 1560.

Like the other Venetian scuole it has two great halls, one on the ground floor and one above, joined by a stair, with a smaller room, the Sala dell'Albergo, where the confraternity's boards met. From 1564 to 1587 Tintoretto and his workshop, among them his son Domenico, painted the canvases for all three. The ground floor tells the life of the Virgin. In the upper hall the Old Testament fills the ceiling and the life of Christ the walls, together the story from the Fall to the Redemption. The Albergo holds his Crucifixion and the Passion. There are also works by Titian.

The scuola was a patron of music as well. Giovanni Gabrieli was its organist, and in 1958 Igor Stravinsky conducted the first performance of his Threni here.
